Librogame.title: In the Blind Spot
Librogame.author: Jérôme Wirth

Changes.Change: Adapted for this app: the structure, the rules and parts of the text were changed or removed to work with its engine
Translated into English from the original French
Added sounds and background music, delivered together with the book

Librogame.ContentWarnings: Drugs, threats, transphobia and homophobia voiced by characters, police violence referred to, the mental illness of a loved one. The narrator is a father out of his depth, and the book doesn't always take his side.
Librogame.Blurb:
2041. A father sets off in search of his runaway daughter, who has vanished into the Socialist Republic of Mexico. That father is YOU.
Down there, mobile technology is banned. You leave your bracelet at customs, you communicate through free-access terminals, you telephone from landlines. You have a photograph, a false name, and nobody to trust.

Variable.name: Actions still possible in Mexico City

Page.Text:
Six months.
It took you six months to get Riwan to spit it out. Six months of hounding him with questions and hearing him first swear blind that he knew nothing. Then confess that he had promised Emilie he would say nothing, and that even though she is your daughter, he had to keep his word. Six months before he broke that word for a few thousand GAFAcoins in his account (but also under the threat of having his homosexuality revealed), and confirmed to you that she had fled under another identity to the Socialist Republic of Mexico.
He was only confirming what looked like your most plausible lead. For two years Emilie had been collecting books about the "Mexican experiment" and never stopped denigrating what she called "reactionary Europe". It was that little bastard Riwan himself who filled her head with it, and it was he who took charge of organising her departure. Without a word. A goodbye. You had understood for some time that Emilie had begun to hate you. Since her mother was committed, in truth. She was an adolescent and there are things she was in no position to understand, still less to accept. With that bitterness eating at you, you raised her as best you could. You too, no doubt, unable to understand her. Nothing extraordinary, as the police made clear to you. Teenage runaways are commonplace, and Mexico an easy destination.
Easy when you don't intend to come back. For you, it meant six more months of waiting before you could arrange a legal stay in the SRM. And it was the Intermetropolis Alliance that put the obstacles in your way, not the Mexicans. Losing track of you for several weeks is a deviation from the norm that requires meticulous precautions. And it's true that the change has something frightening about it. Leaving your bracelet at the customs desk of Mexico City airport. "It will be returned to you when you leave." Agreeing to communicate with your world only through free-access internet terminals. You had to dig up an old email address to be sure of being able to contact your friends.
The Socialist Republic of Mexico prohibits mobile technologies and communicating objects. You can barely use GSM phones, generally for safety reasons, on desert excursions for instance. Most inhabitants make do with the SMS functions anyway.
That is where your daughter has landed herself. And the worst of it is that she may like it. Unless she has met a tragic fate… the Mexican authorities claim they have eradicated crime, but nobody seriously believes them.
You have a photograph of your daughter, and her new identity, which you extorted from Riwan: Sofia Gonzales. It is thin enough to start an investigation with, but one could certainly do worse.

Choice.text: Go and find the Mexican police at the airport
Do without them and look for a hotel

Page.Text:
You notice a small building that serves as both a post office and a souvenir shop. You push through a rope curtain, behind which an affable official points you to a row of old monitors where you can get online. Surprisingly, the connection here is acceptable.
So you set about going through your emails. Nothing notable; it seems your friends already give you up for missing. Although, come to think of it, you haven't been terribly available these last few years, with your wife's illness. Your boss, on the other hand, remembers you perfectly well. He is chasing you about the Servel file and asks you to contact the client urgently. Of course you can only do so by email, and it promises to be thorny. If you get into it, you won't be able to do anything else all evening. But your professional future is at stake. And the unalterable smile of the man behind the counter suggests you have all the time in the world.

Choice.text: Get to work on the Servel file
Get to work on the Servel file

Page.Text:
You show Emilie's photograph to a few locals, but they answer with an apologetic shrug. You do manage to have the House of Culture pointed out to you, a large building on the other side of the square. It serves as the tourist office here, and perhaps they can help you there.
The attendant is smoking a cigarillo under the porch. You plant the photo under his nose and ask whether he has come across this girl. No, he hasn't seen her. So many gringos pass through here, you can't remember them all. Blondes like that, he has seen dozens.
Faced with your crestfallen look, he takes a long draw and thinks for a moment.
Well, quite a few of them take part in the Temazcal ceremony at Dona Cinotta's. They spend time with her, and the old witch has a memory. If your daughter did go to her, she will remember. Otherwise…

You go and find the young man to help with your search, as he kindly offered. You explain that you don't know which end to take your investigation by. He smiles gently and lays a sympathetic hand on your shoulder. An incongruous scene, because you are a head taller than he is.
"Me, comrade, I think you should look at the Casa Libertad. Young foreigners arriving in Mexico City often want to soak up that experience. If your daughter went there, Marcos will remember. I'll take you…"
You nod silently. It will take the two of you about fifteen minutes on foot.

You explain to them that their help is of course welcome, but that you have also turned to a policeman to help with your search. When you describe the circumstances in which you met Lucas, Cassandra's face darkens.
"You shouldn't have done that, comrade. That policeman is a Punisher…
— A Punisher?
— That's what we call the fascist police. Men working quietly towards the destruction of the Socialist Republic and the return of Guzman."
You let out an ironic smile.
"Fascist? Aren't you going a bit far? How could there be fascist police here…
— Don't be naive, comrade. The government couldn't clean out the police from top to bottom. I'd have liked that, believe me. But there are always compromises in the end. Most of the old policemen stayed at their posts.
— But that doesn't mean he's a fascist!
— Believe me. The Punishers are dangerous… for your daughter too."
Juan has stayed silent behind, worried as well. Their anxiety weighs on you.
"I don't understand. Why would Emilie be in danger? They're helping me find her.
— Because… because they hate foreigners. You too, but the volunteers above all. Me, for instance: if they could, they'd kill me.
— It's true, Juan puts in. Look in front of you."
You open the glove compartment and find an automatic pistol. You thought weapons were forbidden here in Mexico.
"I have a dispensation, comrade," Cassandra explains. "The government knows my service record makes me a target for lunatics like your Lucas. Revolutions aren't simple…"
All you see is a weapon, and you aren't obliged to believe that explanation. But what is certain is that things are more complicated than you expected.

The Central Hospital of Mexico City is fairly easy to find and you reach it quickly by metro. You are beginning to feel relatively self-sufficient in this city. That isn't unwelcome, even if you have no intention of prolonging your stay beyond the time needed to find Emilie.
The hospital buildings contrast with the rest of Mexico City. They are almost new, even if they are a long way from European standards of modernity. It must be said that the Mexican Socialist Party takes pride in its health system, modelled on the Castro one. It doesn't stint on spending in that field but, once through the doors, you feel the same sense of dilapidation as everywhere else in the city. No screens to direct patients, no magnetic terminals to check insurance; here you have to speak to the nurses sitting at reception. They are trading jokes, apparently not overworked… as you approach, a nurse of Caribbean origin asks you, in Spanish almost as approximate as your own, what brings you here.
You produce Emilie's photograph, her indelible smile and her blonde hair. You say you think she must have come to this hospital. The young woman's face closes. Yes, it's possible she saw her; European women come through regularly. But the hospital is bound by medical confidentiality, it's very difficult to help you. The other two nurses nod silently.
An old man on a walking frame has come closer. He listens to your exchange attentively, his eye twinkling, as if he were about to burst out laughing. You try to ignore him and to rein in your irritation.

Lucas has left you a message asking you to meet him as quickly as possible at the "Pax Romana". You feverishly pull on your blazer and hurry off towards the bar.
It's the afternoon, but the room is as dark as ever. There is no girl on the floor and only a few customers sipping cocktails. Lucas is waiting at his table, smoothing his skull with a nervous hand. His manner tempers your excitement. His eyes slip away each time you seek them, and he insists on buying you a tequila. Little remains of the virile assurance of your first meeting.
Finally he launches into his explanation, head lowered. He has located Emilie. He told you he'd find her, that much was certain. He sketches a slight smile, quickly drowned in a mouthful of tequila. He put some men on "recovering" her for you. From experience, these girls refuse to return to the family fold unless you force them a little…
At this point in his account you feel like shouting at him. You are paying him to find your daughter, not to organise a kidnapping! But you stay silent. You wait anxiously for what comes next.
There was a problem. Emilie (he pauses) … your daughter fell in with the wrong people. It often goes like that. They were armed and they defended themselves. Lucas gives you to understand that "his boys" are far from gentle either, then he seems to slide off the words. As if reality were so soaped over that no sentence could get a grip on it any more.
He is sorry. Unfortunately these things happen. Of course there is no longer any question of money… all he can advise is that you go back to Europe and forget you ever set foot in Mexico. You wouldn't have liked what she had become, that much he can tell you.
The last sentences reach you muffled by a black veil. The reflections of the bottles and the mirrors, the rectangle of the television, everything fades into a dizzying dance. You sink into the chasm that has been holding out its arms to you for many years already.

You notice a folded piece of paper on the floor. Evidently fallen from your jacket. Intrigued, you pick it up. A note scrawled by hand.
The police will not help you find your daughter. If you want someone to take care of it, come to the Pax Romana tonight at nine. Ask for Lucas.
Your stay isn't starting so badly after all. Help, any help, can be welcome. Even if by nature you remain wary of mysterious strangers who want what's best for you… at the very least, nothing is free in this world. But you have money with you.
In any case it isn't too late to keep that appointment.

Choice.text: Ignore this lead and go to bed

Page.Text: Juan comes to find you. He tells you he has to go back up to Mexico City with his girlfriend Cassandra this very morning. He suggests you go back up with them, if you have nothing more to do here. Otherwise you'll have to take the bus.

Choice.text: Get back to Mexico City under your own steam

Page.Text:
At reception all is quiet. The receptionist is finishing a crossword, fanned by the creaking to and fro of a ceiling fan. She is delighted to help when you show her the photo of your daughter. But she quickly makes it clear she has no memory of this blonde girl.
At that moment a young man in fatigues and a cap approaches you. A round, youthful face, set off by a thin moustache. He addresses you in English, with a strong accent, but not a Spanish one.
"Looking for your daughter, comrade? If you like, I can act as your guide."
The receptionist nods and stresses that the young man, one Juan, knows the city very well and is used to escorting foreigners. You look again at this man who does indeed seem to be an emissary of the Party, his bearing too stiff for a boy who looks barely out of puberty.
After all, why not? In any case you can always call on his services if need be.
So here you are, back in Mexico City. The information you managed to glean in Temoaya has not advanced your search a great deal. What will you do now?

Choice.text: Go to the Mexico City hospital
Find a public telephone and make a call
Rest and read in your room
Contact your guide to ask for his help

Page.Text:
"Sofia Gonzales?"
The policeman is shaken by a nervous snigger that makes his lip and his moustache jump. He searches the airport registers.
"Listen, comrade. I can tell you she landed here in September 2040, coming from Paris. There. Beyond that, I can't be any more use. What she does here is none of my business.
— Don't tell me you don't keep track of foreigners on your territory?
— Sofia Gonzales has Mexican nationality, as far as I can judge. And even if she were foreign it wouldn't change much."
You bite your lips.
"You must surely know where she lives!
— There are certainly departments that know. For my part I have no access to that information. And that means Señora Gonzales doesn't wish anyone to have access to it, comrade.
— But she's my daughter!
— Yes, you told me. Listen, comrade, if she were a minor we could have done something. We wouldn't have let her into the country like that, for a start. But if she chose to change her life in Mexico, that is the choice of a responsible adult. If you want to find her, you'll have to do it by your own means. People here are quite open. It isn't impossible…"
He hands back the photograph with a small, uneasy smile. With a sigh you rest your eyes on Emilie's blonde, chubby-cheeked face. The Mexican police will not help you. But it is still better that they admit their incompetence straight away rather than waste your time. And at least this official spoke French.

Lucas has left you a message asking you to call him back this evening. So you pick up the old telephone handset provided and dial his number.
His voice is rather nasal in the earpiece, but you manage to make out what the policeman wants to tell you. His informers have given him a first report. Emilie stayed at the Casa Libertad, remaining there about ten days. Then she took the bus to a small town called Temoaya. There she intended to attend the Temazcal ceremony at the camp of one Dona Cinotta. You scribble this down on the notepad you slipped into your luggage. You curse the pen's ink, which half refuses to flow.
You ask Lucas whether he can go with you to Temoaya but he refuses flatly. He is a policeman. And a real cop, as you can see, not a slacker. He has work to do. And besides, he has nothing to do with those backward Indians and their old witch. In any case they'll surely be more talkative with you; they're used to foreigners. There is a bus leaving for Temoaya every day. You can tell him what you found when you get back and then we'll see. He mumbles a goodbye and hangs up.

Juan takes you into a vast shed housing a hundred or so cars. You cross the threshold of a blockhouse where an official has you fill in a register. You sign beneath Juan.
Then your guide collects the magnetic key and shows you your vehicle. An electric car. Two seats and a boot. The sort of thing that can't do more than fifty miles an hour. The journey will no doubt be more comfortable than by coach, but certainly longer.
Juan takes the wheel. You leave Mexico City and take the main road. It is fairly well maintained, but you mostly pass coaches and scooters. Very few cars.
"We're privileged, if I understand correctly…"
Juan's face closes.
"Not really. Anyone can borrow these vehicles, in case of compelling need. I explained to the keeper that you were looking for your missing daughter and he judged that a valid reason. Was I wrong, perhaps, comrade?"
You regret your sarcastic tone. After all, this boy is making himself very useful. And what's more he makes the effort to address you in English. A language in which you can hold a real conversation.
"No. Thank you, Juan."
You ask whether he is a "volunteer" and he nods.
"Which country are you from?
— I'm Mexican, comrade.
— I mean, what origin?
— That doesn't matter any more.
— You left your family, like my daughter?
— Yes.
— Is that why you want to help me?
— Perhaps, comrade. But here, helping others is a duty."
Juan sinks into a pensive silence. The kilometres go by under a blue sky in which only a few clouds fray lazily. Then you stop, beside what seems to be a cantina.
"Are we there?
— Not yet, comrade. But the car needs charging. We'll take the chance to have lunch. I'm paying.
— There's no need, Juan. I have money."
You wave your wallet.
"I'm paying, comrade."
The young man has laid his hand on your forearm. The situation becomes awkward and he blushes before withdrawing it. Slightly disconcerted, you follow him into the dimness of the room and take a seat at a table in silence.
The landlady sings the praises of native Mexican maize, GMO-free of course, and brings you a dish containing that famous foodstuff. It's good, but it's still maize. The mango for dessert, on the other hand, is delicious.
Juan has a phone call to make. He points out that an internet connection is available on the other side of the room, just in case, then slips away towards the bar. Getting online isn't a bad idea, but on the other hand a trip to the toilets wouldn't hurt.

Choice.text: Go to the toilets, behind the bar
Wait for Juan and take the road to Temoaya again

Page.Text:
The Casa Libertad matches what you were told. A sort of old boarding house with a canteen and showers upstairs. You do the cooking and the cleaning yourself, preferably in a group. That is what Libna, a young Algerian woman, explains with overflowing enthusiasm. The group welcoming you is young. Were it not for a couple of Norwegian pensioners with unalterable smiles, you would be the eldest. You have confirmation that the place isn't made for you, but that Emilie would necessarily have felt at home here.
You are allowed to choose a room. They are all identical, with a white metal bed and a bedside table topped by a lamp made from a bottle. At least they are clean and aired. You do your share of the kitchen duty like everyone else. Libna has taken command and explains in her approximate English how to prepare a tagine. You volunteer to peel the potatoes. At least this activity empties your mind for a while.
The meal is also taken communally, in the refectory. But nobody will stop you withdrawing to your room with a plate. You brought a book to read anyway.

Another good quarter of an hour's wait before a woman appears. A tall, lanky redhead who approaches with long strides. Anglo-Saxon type. Juan gets up and embraces her. The two lovers share a passionate kiss. The woman is a good head taller than he is, and ten years older no doubt.
After that embrace, her hand makes a bunch of keys glitter and she goes to open the door of the house. None of this looks like a conspiracy. Juan has a romantic assignation in Temoaya… He still shoots up, though.
You can, if you wish, leave your hiding place and recover the syringe as evidence against Juan. You never know…

Choice.text: Recover the syringe, then find the lovers and apologise
Recover the syringe, then look for a room for the night
Leave the syringe and find the lovers
Leave the syringe and look for a room for the night

Page.Text:
Your emails consist almost exclusively of demands from your boss. A big client is complaining about your lack of responsiveness, and yet it isn't for want of having made clear that you were going on leave! Nobody seems capable of taking over for you on this matter, nor on the others for that matter…
You can spend time trying to defuse the situation.

Choice.text: Do some research on Dr Santorini
Catch up on the latest European news

Page.Text:
The Gran Hotel lives up to its name. The adjective "gran", at least. For the rest, you feel more as if you were in a department store on the boulevard Haussmann than in a hotel. It's true that the Samaritaine is a hotel these days…
The decor is sumptuous and space is not lacking. Too much space. You chose to stay here telling yourself you would be more comfortable. A hotel designed for Western tourists in the Socialist Republic of Mexico. Except that you had forgotten there are practically no Western tourists in Mexico. If you aren't the only guest, the others hide themselves well.
You pass only employees, dressed in blue cloth, with an indolent, not to say mocking, air. At least your room is undeniably comfortable, and you know you don't have to pay any tips. Wages are covered by the Party.
You even have television, for want of a wireless connection. But you didn't come here to watch programmes about the agrarian revolution, or whatever else…
You throw your jacket onto the console table and consider what you intend to do.

Choice.text: Go down to reception and ask about the city

Page.Text:
From his stammering voice when you tell him about your search, you quickly understand that Dr Santorini is shaken. You have to ask him more than once to repeat himself.
He begins by telling you about the Punisher. The man paid him a visit because of you. You have no idea what you have set off! After a while you understand that the person he calls the Punisher is none other than Lucas. He apparently threatened the lives of his two daughters — children of six and eight — to obtain information about Emilie. Santorini then spilled it: Emilie has changed sex.
The news leaves you speechless…
The doctor hurries to shake you out of it. You must absolutely find him now! Those Punisher dogs deeply hate homosexuals, lesbians, transsexuals… you must fear for your son's life.
Panicked, you ask him how you can find her now. Has he kept her contact details? Unfortunately, the doctor explains that this kind of operation is generally followed by a change of identity. And the Mexican state permits the deletion of data corresponding to the former identity. Sofia Gonzales has, so to speak, never existed, and Emilie hasn't been in touch with him since. He must be followed by a clinic for his hormone treatment, under his new identity. His face has certainly changed. And he may have dyed his hair. Or not. The only piece of information he can give you nonetheless is that Emilie intended to change her age too. Thirty years old.
That was the age he wanted to show, rather than his twenty-two. Thirty… a very thin clue!
The police always keep a record of identity changes, though… and that is precisely what worries Santorini. Lucas should manage to pick up the trail fairly quickly if he can get access to the files. He insists: Emilie is in danger. Your hands tremble on the handset.
And don't go back to Lucas!
So here you are, condemned to succeed… or to hope that this doctor doesn't know what he's talking about.

Evenings at the Casa consist of drinking alcohol and putting the world to rights. It's an exercise in which you have some experience, perhaps more than your companions. But generally it's with your close friends, single men if not confirmed bachelors. A habit you took up again after your wife was committed. And even more after Emilie disappeared.
So you have no trouble lining up the tequilas, but you keep a certain reserve towards all this exuberant youth. A group of Congolese enliven the evening with music and singing. They are perhaps the only ones who haven't fled their own country. The conversation runs on the future of the Mexican revolution, the genetic preservation of maize and all the achievements the "volunteers" have taken part in. Off to one side, two boys are kissing.
A Vietnamese woman barely twenty years old has sat down beside you. She lays a hand on your arm and asks what you think of it all. You dispel the fog invading your mind. This is the sort of opportunity you were looking for. You explain that the revolution is a bit remote from you. You are looking for your daughter, who ran away from France. You even show her the photo. She seems disappointed but she is good-hearted and signals to a man called Marco.
Marco is a regular here. He stays here more or less permanently. He is connected to the Party. If anyone can help you, it's him. He studies the photobooth picture, drawing on a cigarillo. For an interminable time.
Yes, he saw her, no doubt about it. The girl came from France. He now looks you over with curiosity, pushing aside the curtain of his hair with a practised hand. Yes, she stayed about ten days at the Casa. Then she took the bus to Temoaya. A trip for a sort of spiritual retreat. Many foreigners do that. Libna laughs and assures you it's a "compulsory rite". You can take the bus tomorrow if you like. Or another day if you prefer. The Otomi are welcoming.
Finally Thuy-Nun, the young Vietnamese woman, walks you to your room. She explains with nervous volubility why she fled her parents, the promise of bourgeois comfort… for a moment you think she wants to make you feel guilty, but she has no ulterior motive. Not of that kind, at any rate.
She is sitting on your bed and you list in your head the reasons why you will not sleep with her tonight: you have drunk too much; you are exhausted from the journey; you could be her father; she could be your daughter…
You slump onto the bed.
Daylight assaults you around ten in the morning. You have a slight headache, but it could have been worse. Thuy-Nun has wisely gone back to her own room.

Through the flat's window you make out two silhouettes in the street below. You immediately recognise Juan and his partner Cassandra, in military fatigues. They are talking and smiling. Juan spots you and waves. You hesitate to wave back. The couple followed you here, undoubtedly. For what reason? To show you the Party has its eye on you? Or perhaps it's Lucas who interests them…

You knock at the door and let them know you saw Juan in the street. Juan seems genuinely delighted to see you again. Oddly, he doesn't seem to hold the cantina episode against you; he doesn't even want to bring it up when you stammer out implausible excuses. Above all he is eager to introduce his partner, Cassandra.
The woman offers you a vigorous handshake while Juan explains that she is a real "volunteer". Cassandra is lovely, her face scattered with freckles. Her eyes plant themselves in yours with an intimidating frankness. They invite you to stay for dinner, but you have no intention of imposing. You say you are going to find a room for the night before resuming your search tomorrow.
You still have time to think it over between now and tomorrow morning.

Otherwise you fall back on the Ian Manook thriller you brought just in case. There isn't much entertainment in Mexico City, though you might one day try one of those old cinemas restored by the government.

Choice.text: Take a look at the book

Page.Text:
Your search has been stalling for several days. You have combed the shops and the most popular cantinas without obtaining any more information. Dispirited, you decide to turn yourself into a "tourist". Even if the term is thoroughly inappropriate here, the Mexican tourist industry having been swept away by the advent of the Socialist Republic. It is more a matter of making the most of what Mexico City can offer you, by putting yourself in the shoes of a young volunteer who has just arrived. Your first choice falls on a repair workshop. Many inhabitants have recommended these places, apparently convivial, where the young and the not-so-young gather, some of them almost daily.
When you cross the threshold of one of them, you are immediately caught up in the effervescent atmosphere. Conversations are in full flow and at first nobody pays you any attention. On one side, the traditional workshop gathers the older ones around ancient pieces of machinery. Here they repair watches, alarm clocks, hi-fi systems, with screwdrivers and soldering irons. A few printed-circuit specialists are besieged by requests from their neighbours. A bicycle room occupies the back of the workshop. On the other side are the 3D printers, humming without interruption, operated by teenagers or adults in their thirties. It is towards these machines that you head, and you are welcomed willingly.
The Socialist Republic isn't entirely hostile to modernity, apparently. All these young people are highly skilled at designing parts of every kind, which will be used by the other workshops to replace broken or missing equipment. They explain that the paste used is mainly a compound of maize and milk, which reduces harmful fumes in the room. But for the most durable parts, polluting substances are needed… you thus spend two hours designing keys and a casing for a computer keyboard. The young man who took you in hand to explain how the machine works is called Juan. Despite his jet-black hair, his skin is too pale for a Mexican, and his hesitant accent confirms that he is probably a volunteer. His military-toned clothing confirms his commitment, if confirmation were needed. When you have finished your work, the result astonishes even you, and Juan applauds sincerely.
"That's very good for a newcomer… you must come back here, comrade!"
The two of you go on talking, and you tell him about Emilie. He invites you to sit in a corner, next to a pile of magazines.
"It's common here, parents looking for their children… we can help, but you also have to respect the wishes of those who want to change their lives. But you know what? I'm inviting you to dinner at my place. I'm moving in with my girlfriend, Cassandra. She's a volunteer too, she's moved around a lot. We can talk about it over a good meal… what do you say?"
This young man's candour and spontaneity put you at ease. After all, you have no much better option than to entrust yourself to willing people who know the ground. So you accept his invitation.

Doctor Hernan Santorini is indeed a physician at the Central Hospital of Mexico City, specialising in plastic and reconstructive surgery.
Emilie's face, disfigured by an accident — a fire? —, prints itself violently on your brain. Your pulse quickens and a dark veil crosses your field of vision. You struggle to get your breath back, leaning on the table.
Of course not. If Emilie had been disfigured, Dona Cinotta wouldn't have recognised her in the photograph. And she already had Dr Santorini's contact details. On the other hand, you do think you know Emilie well enough to know she isn't the type to resort to cosmetic surgery. She never attached much importance to her femininity. And besides, why would she have fled to Mexico for that? There are so many specialists in Europe.
Your breathing is normal again and you try to take things calmly.
Nothing tells you that her dealings with this Santorini have anything to do with medicine. You examine the doctor's photograph — he looks about forty, with advanced baldness — and it inspires nothing in you but disgust. The idea of imagining Emilie with that…
Right. Short of asking the man himself, you see no way of calming your palpitations. After a slightly deeper search, you dig up what does indeed seem to be Dr Santorini's personal telephone number. That might be more effective than a visit to the hospital!

A farmer offers to drop you at Dona Cinotta's camp in a van. The camp lies outside the town, not far from the Centro Ceremonial Otomí, and you follow a bumpy road. You come within sight of a village of bungalows. A fairly young group is sitting in the shade of a tree. Meditating, apparently.
Dona Cinotta leaves her "students" for a moment to come and find you. She is an Indian woman in her fifties. Her loose dress covers a generous bosom, drawing a rounder silhouette than she probably has. She draws on a bone pipe while listening to your story and nods to punctuate your sentences.
She doesn't need to look at the photo for long. That girl, of course she saw her. She stayed a week at the camp and took part in the Temazcal ceremony. You walk with her a while towards the earthen sweat lodge where the ceremony takes place. Dona Cinotta launches into a barely comprehensible account of the purification rite. Purification of the body. But above all purification of the soul, she insists.
With her hands she describes the dome the lodge forms and explains that it is also a woman's womb. The Temazcal is practised when great decisions are taken. It is a second birth. Of course, there are those who do it purely for fun. But your daughter had taken a decision.
Unfortunately she stayed very vague about what she was looking for. A fresh start, of course. Like all the volunteers who leave their country. But something else. Dona Cinotta felt it. Emilie asked her a great many questions about shamans and sorcerers, about the transformation of the soul. She was reading a book by Carlos Castaneda. Like so many gringos.
Quite a swindler, that Castaneda. A brilliant swindler, perhaps, but a swindler. Dona Cinotta could have introduced her to real sorcerers. But what would they have done with a little Western girl brandishing Castaneda?
She bursts into a coarse laugh that betrays too much tobacco. Then she stops and looks at you. The book! Of course, she had forgotten it.
She trots off towards a wooden house that must be her home. She comes back out of breath with the book in her hand.
It may not be much use to you. It's all she can do to help.
You examine the cover. The Art of Dreaming, by Carlos Castaneda. Hard to imagine what this book with its worn spine could teach you about Emilie's journey. You pocket it all the same.
Emilie left after a week and Dona Cinotta supposes she went back to Mexico City. Which, all in all, brings you back to square one.

Choice.text: Take the bus back to Mexico City

Page.Text:
When Juan comes to fetch you, he seems shaken. You let him sit down for a moment and he explains, his voice trembling, the events of the last few hours. He and his partner were the victims of an attack.
"You understand, comrade. There are still so many people in this country who'd like to have the hide of a volunteer like Cassandra. She fought with Fîrya Behwan, you know…"
He lets out a proud smile.
"Luckily, she shoots better than they do!"
You start. So there was an exchange of gunfire! And Juan's partner shot men dead. You suddenly realise that this country, beneath its peaceable surface, ultimately hides an everyday violence. That can only worry you further about Emilie.
"Look, Juan, I think the best thing is to put this dinner off…
— Are you joking, comrade? Cassandra only has a superficial wound, a bullet that grazed her shoulder. She's making the tortillas right now. You wouldn't want her to cook for nothing, would you?"
Juan puts on a forced enthusiasm, but you have no argument to offer against it. Even if it turns out that you may be the one most worried by this whole business…

The Pax Romana is a men's bar. Setting aside the stripper swaying on the stage, of course. You doubt this kind of show is genuinely to the taste of the Mexican Socialist Party, and you assume this dive is more or less clandestine.
An exclusively male clientele is drinking beer and tequila and applauding the dancer, who replies with sensual kisses. But nobody goes near her. You ask for Lucas, and you are taken to a small round table where a young man sits, legs apart. Cropped hair and three days' stubble. A black bomber jacket covered in patches.
The conversation is painful given your level of Spanish, but you understand that Lucas is himself a policeman. He doesn't share the Socialist Party's views, but as he puts it he is "a cop in his soul". You aren't the only one looking for a missing child in Mexico, and he and his friends try to help foreign parents. Because he reckons that is what his "cop's job" really is. Of course, as you had foreseen, it isn't free. There are expenses.
Two thousand GAFAcoins to be paid into an account Lucas holds in Los Angeles. When the job is done, and once you're back in Europe, because here you won't be able to, of course. He trusts you, all the more so since he has friends in the police in Europe, he adds with a wink. Later he'll collect that money, when he and his friends have brought down the Party of bitches, as he calls them. Or else Lucas will go to the United States.
The sum he demands isn't a problem for you. The question is: do you trust him? Which raises another question, incidentally: do you have any other option?
Either way, you then go back to spend the night at the hotel you chose.
You sit down on the bed, which creaks slightly, and open the book. An old thriller by Ian Manook. That should keep you occupied for the evening.
What will you do now?

Choice.text: Enquire at the Gran Hotel reception
Question the manager of the Casa Libertad

Page.Text:
You take the book out of the bag. A paperback you have already seen in Emilie's hands, without ever really paying attention to it. Dona Cinotta described Castaneda to you as a swindler, and it's true that this little volume on the art of dreaming resembles a fable more than an autobiography. The enigmatic character of Don Juan is certainly designed to arouse the Western reader's curiosity, and you try to put yourself in the skin of a teenage girl for whom mysterious doors are opening onto an infinite spiritual universe. But the effort soon tires you and, after a few dozen pages, you content yourself with leafing through it carelessly… at which point you come upon a note scrawled on a scrap of paper, slipped between two pages. The handwriting is Emilie's: "Pr. Santorini, Central Hospital Mexico City"
Why did your daughter write down that name? The best way is surely to find out what she had to do at the hospital. The irruption of this unhoped-for clue puts an end to your interest in this reading, and you throw the book on the floor.

As you take your leave of the official, a minibus stops on the other side of the square and you catch sight of Juan's slight silhouette stepping calmly down from it. The boy is stubborn. He followed you all the way here! He adjusts his cap and turns into an alley on the right. He doesn't seem to be looking for you in particular…
After all, he did say he had business in Temoaya. Pricked by curiosity, you rather want to follow him and find out at last what he's up to. But you won't have time to go to Dona Cinotta's this evening.

Choice.text: Follow the lead from the man with the cigarillo

Page.Text:
On the way you pass behind Juan, glued to the telephone handset. He hasn't noticed you. He is deep in conversation with someone visibly close to him. He is trying to hold back bursts of laughter.
No, he suspects nothing. Of course. Everything will be fine.
Is Juan talking about you? What situation have you got yourself into? You know nothing about this young man, who may be charged with keeping an eye on you for the Party. Unless he is acting on behalf of people even less recommendable. For a long time Mexico was the kidnappers' paradise, with astronomical ransoms demanded for the children of the upper middle class. That class has fled the country for good, but the scum is still there.
Juan has left the car keys and the booking log on the table. You have the chance to slip away and leave him here.
Otherwise you prefer to trust him, to go to the toilets and come back to wait at the table before setting off again for Temoaya.

Choice.text: Slip away and leave him here
Trust him and go back to the table

Page.Text:
You feel a little old-fashioned having to dial a number on a landline, while wondering whether Santorini will actually be at home at this hour. How can a society still function without offering a smooth way of reaching people? Perplexed, you count the rings. One, two, three… someone picks up.
You quickly confirm that it is indeed Dr Santorini, rather astonished, at the other end of the line.
Otherwise all you get from Santorini is a scolding which, in his agitation, is half unintelligible. You do grasp that Westerners really do think they can do as they please. If your daughter wanted to start her life over here, it isn't for him to betray her secrets! Without further ado, he hangs up on you.

The square of Temoaya. Facing the church, which casts its ochre bell tower against the azure of the sky. This is the territory of the Otomí people. It's bad enough that you barely manage in Spanish; adding the Indians' accent is torture for you.

Choice.text: Go straight to the place you were told about
Begin your search in the square

Page.Text:
So here you are, left to your own devices in Mexico City. What's more, without an automatic translator. You will have to gather the rusty remains of your school Spanish to see your search through. The exit visa expires in thirty days. Of course, the Mexicans won't expel you. But the return to Europe risks becoming very complicated if you overrun that deadline.
Your first destination will be a hotel. First because you need one, but above all because you imagine Emilie must have gone through the same. Unless someone was waiting for her. Riwan didn't seem to think so and he isn't brave enough to deceive you outright. But Emilie may not have told him everything.
You flag down a taxi and manage to make the driver understand that you're looking for a hotel. Not too expensive but comfortable enough, in the heart of Mexico City if possible. You know that, in any case, the hotels of the big Western chains have all been converted into housing. The driver, a burly mestizo, waves a hand with a broad smile to let you know he has just the address.
Gran Hotel de Mexico. Foreigners love it. There are even computers with internet.
On the off chance, you ask whether there are any more "socialist" hotels. The driver's smile widens further and he points you to the Casa Libertad. Apparently a sort of hostel self-managed by those who live there. Popular with foreigners in search of the "Mexican experience". Typically the sort of thing that would appeal to Emilie. Not necessarily your sort of thing.

Marcos is, so to speak, the manager of the Casa Libertad. The term is inappropriate, of course, since the hostel is self-managed. Except that Marcos lives there permanently. And you rather suspect he is the Party's eye. But after all, in this country, to find someone you certainly have to go through the Mexican Socialist Party at some point.
The young man greets you with a polite smile and examines the photobooth picture you show him. He frowns.
Yes, he saw her, no doubt about it. The girl came from France. He now looks you over with curiosity, pushing aside the curtain of his hair with a practised hand. Yes, she stayed about ten days at the Casa. Then she took the bus to Temoaya. A trip for a sort of spiritual retreat. Many foreigners do that.
Here is an investigation moving forward almost beyond hope.

Juan's youthful face rounds into a crinkling of the eyes that you know well. Too well.
"Tell me, Juan, how old are you?
— Thirty-one, as of recently. People always tell me I look younger.
— That's true."
Mentally you erase that moustache whose too-deep black clashes with his pale skin, barely browned under the sun's harassment. You imagine two blue eyes. And those too-slender fingers…
You murmur:
"Emilie…
— My name is Juan.
— The syringe. The hormone treatment. It's you!"
You shouted. Juan lets go of your arm, hesitant, but the smile hasn't left him. On the other side of the counter, Cassandra pretends to be interested only in the cutlery and the plates she has in fact finished washing.
"Stop this game, Emilie. All this time I thought I was looking for you, when it was you spying on me! Don't you think it would have been simpler to tell me everything?"
Juan lets out a sigh, and you can almost touch his immense relief.
"Of course it wouldn't have been simpler! I had to be sure… we had to be sure you'd accept Juan. When Riwan told me you were coming…
— Riwan, that little worm! He sold you for GAFAcoins.
— Riwan did what I asked him to. He's the one who put me in touch with Professor Santorini, since apparently you traced him. He warned me you were coming, and we chose this method… to put your child right in front of your eyes and see whether you'd recognise him!"
You stay silent, petrified with shame. Son or daughter, you didn't recognise him. His expressions, his smile… his convictions. And there is so much you failed to see! You get up, convinced there is nothing left but to withdraw. Juan holds you back. And Cassandra judges that it is time to take her place at the table again.
"You took your time, Dad, but it doesn't matter at all. And the evening is only beginning…"
Cassandra pours you another glass of pulque.
Juan needs to talk. Or rather Emilie, through him. Needs to tell you how much the teenager she was resented you when her mother had to be committed. She thought you hadn't done enough for her, hadn't known how to handle her depression. You were too taken up with your work. On that much you can't say he is wrong. You reproached yourself for it, but you never knew how to get out of that alienating routine which at least let you put together the money you needed for yourself, your wife, your daughter…
That is why she left, but not only that. Emilie tells you she eventually understood that you couldn't have done better. She understood that her mother was sick from her own dreams. Sick from not having at her fingertips everything modern civilisation promised, a life always better, always different… and that was what she wanted to flee. A world which, in her words, did nothing any more but sell dreams and legal drugs. She wanted to step squarely into the reality of her century.
You listen attentively. Honestly, it may be the first time you have seriously weighed Emilie's arguments… Juan's arguments. There is an underlying truth, as always with her. Your life is nothing but a succession of routines, occupations and entertainments. Nothing more extraordinary than what can be found here, when it comes down to it. And yet all that talk of greatness, of progress…
On the other hand, don't the volunteers come here too to live a waking dream? Is it realistic, plausible, to hold oneself apart from this modernity? And that operation, the subject Juan has been deliberately avoiding all evening — isn't it the culmination of the society of dreams?
But for tonight, you have no wish to argue.

A folded piece of paper slips out of a pocket of your jacket and bounces on the floor. You pick it up with curiosity, certain that you weren't the one who put it there. A note scrawled by hand.
The police will not help you find your daughter. If you want someone to take care of it, come to the Pax Romana tonight at nine. Ask for Lucas.
Your stay isn't starting so badly after all. Help, any help, can be welcome. Even if by nature you remain wary of mysterious strangers who want what's best for you… at the very least, nothing is free in this world. But you have money with you.

Juan drops by this morning and you tell him about Temoaya.
"Temoaya? I have business there as it happens. If you like, I can borrow a car and take you, comrade. It'll save you the bus journey. Foreigners often appreciate a bit more comfort."
He smiles knowingly. The offer is tempting, but on the other hand you don't know much about this man. Isn't he expecting something from you? Is it a good idea to depend on him?

You produce the syringe and explain to the nurses that you saw a "volunteer" using it, certainly to take drugs. You can't hold back a mocking smile, to make it quite clear that you aren't taken in by the government's propaganda about eradicating the drug trade. Incredulous, the nurses signal to a man in fatigues, who approaches silently, hands clasped behind his back. They exchange a few quick words in Spanish, eyes fixed on the syringe, then the man asks them to have it analysed.
The old man on the walking frame is now sniggering openly, revealing his toothless jaw. You resolutely ignore him and follow the object's progress, placed in an airtight plastic bag, then in a labelled envelope, and finally taken in hand by a man in charge of the post.
You go and sit down next to a woman and her children. You want to wait here for the result of the analysis. Not only to enjoy the discomfiture of all these devotees of the Mexican revolution. You want to be clear about what you can expect from Juan. If need be, you'll denounce him, even if the prospect hardly delights you.
The wait lasts several hours. At last a nurse comes to find you and hands back the syringe in its plastic bag, along with a slip of paper marked with an 8 scrawled in red felt-tip. In an angry tone she explains that of course it isn't drugs. The syringe contained testosterone, and she makes it clear that you shouldn't have meddled in that person's private life. The man in fatigues watches you from a distance with a disabused look.
You get up without a word and leave the hospital. For you there is little doubt: these officials wanted to protect a volunteer, and to protect the Party. You could have expected it, for that matter. But you had hoped professional conscience would win out. Never mind.
Or else… Juan would be injecting himself with testosterone.

For the return journey Juan has this time borrowed a five-seater. The car has a spacious boot, in which the couple have piled some belongings, a coffee table and a small fridge in particular. Cassandra is driving and Juan has sat in the back, leaving you the other front seat. He leans forward on your seats and, all smiles, joins the conversation.
Cassandra answers your questions about her past as a volunteer willingly.
"So it's true that you fought against the drug traffickers?
— It's true, comrade."
Juan gives her a shove, laughing.
"Show him, darling, if he doesn't believe you!"
With one hand Cassandra lifts the back of her blouse and reveals an expanse of white skin punched through by a wide red scar, above the hip. A bullet mark, apparently.
"Many left their skin there. It isn't a legend to seduce Westerners.
— But there's something I don't understand. Why you? Why couldn't the Mexicans have handled it themselves? They can fight…
— When you know the situation, you quickly see why. We volunteers gave up everything: our country, our family, our friends… we had nothing to lose. The narcos didn't hesitate to kill or maim the children of those who opposed them. Don't think the Mexicans are cowards, comrade!
— I didn't say that.
— We were an army. More than that. Brothers and sisters, all united in the fight. And they had no hold over us.
— I'm sorry, but I feel as if I'm hearing the speech of the jihadists of the Caliphate of Amman."
Silence falls in the car. Nothing can be heard but the dull noise of the tyres rolling. In the end it is Juan who speaks.
"You can't say that, comrade, you can't.
— Leave him, Cassandra replies. I know the Westerners' line well. You're only interested in the form and not the content.
— I don't understand.
— Nobody fights for nothing, comrade. Neither us nor the jihadists. And most fighters resemble one another, it's true… but the question is what one fights for. The Mexican people know what we fought for. They haven't forgotten. And if you ended up allying yourselves with the jihadists, it's no accident! It's because of the content of our struggle.
— Well, all that's a question of point of view.
— Yes. And what if I told you that back in Europe the rich bourgeois drink the blood of infants to grant themselves eternal youth?"
You burst out laughing.
"That's nonsense! It's synthetic blood… I've tasted it, it's rather sickening. It costs a fortune but apparently it really is good for the skin. That's what the scientists say, at any rate.
— All that is a question of point of view, comrade."
You rather regret having killed the mood, but Cassandra's moralising line irritates you in the highest degree. You heard too much of it from Emilie. But you have to admit she is brave. And she isn't lacking in charm. You think back bitterly on the years spent with your wife sinking into depression. When she had every comfort one could dream of. You find yourself almost jealous of Juan.
Your guide suggests putting on the radio to lighten the atmosphere. You finish the journey listening to songs, most of them very old. On one of them (an A-ha song) Juan and Cassandra join in the words and even finish the last verse at the top of their voices: "So if you're careful you won't get hurt, but if you're careful all the time, then what's it worth?"
You could laugh at the situation but you feel strangely at ease. As if the two lovers had made a point of taking you into their family.
You reach the outskirts of Mexico City. Stopped at a red light. Cassandra fixes you with her eyes, as she did yesterday.
"I really hope you find your… Emilie… that's right, isn't it? Juan will go on helping you, won't he?"
Juan nods.

It's been several hours since you were last online. You go to check your emails. You have a flood of them. More than you'll have time to read properly. You skim the senders and note that you already have two messages from your boss. He is asking you to contact a client about a file you are the only one to know in detail.
You sigh. You suspected this sort of demand would crop up. Never mind the leave. But if you comply, you'll ruin the evening.

Choice.text: Let it go and head down to reception

Page.Text:
Juan isn't worried about whether he is being followed. Just as well, because shadowing people isn't your profession! You keep a respectful distance, then tuck yourself into a recess between two houses when the young man decides to sit down on the steps of an old house. From there you watch him easily, trying not to arouse the neighbours' suspicions.
Your guide seems to be waiting for someone here. After a few minutes he shows signs of impatience, then takes a case from his jacket pocket. He rolls up one sleeve, takes out a syringe and gives himself an injection in the arm. In the middle of the street. He stands up, throws the syringe into a bin. Then he returns to his waiting position and adjusts his sleeve.
The official propaganda of the Mexican Socialist Party holds that drug trafficking has been definitively eradicated. The war waged by the "volunteers" against the traffickers is even the subject of an elaborate mythology among those interested in the new Mexican paradise. Emilie was among the first to extol to you the courage of those expatriates who faced, weapons in hand, the paramilitary groups financed by the narcos.
The unofficial version circulating in the West is less glorious. While the narcos were indeed brought to their knees, the production of narcotics was not abandoned but taken over by the Party itself to subsidise its policies.
The scene you have just witnessed speaks for itself.

Choice.text: Look for a room for the night
Find out who Juan is waiting for

Page.Text:
You have no trouble getting the coach stop for Temoaya pointed out to you. Hiring a car is almost impossible, especially for a foreigner. Ten people are already waiting. An old lady indicates with her fingers that there is no more than ten minutes to wait.
Forty minutes later the coach appears at the end of the street. There are now a good twenty of you at the stop.
During the journey you are barely sitting on your seat. Crushed, rather, between two passengers calling to each other over your head. Two hours on the road under the sun, with the air conditioning off. Luckily the asphalt is fairly well maintained.
One of your neighbours offers you grilled maize. After some hesitation you accept. You explain that you are looking for your daughter. She went to Temoaya a long time ago. As it happens, that's where he lives. You show him the photo but he shakes his head. No, he hasn't seen her, he doesn't think so. But so many "volunteers" come to stay in Temoaya. Your daughter will surely have attended the Temazcal ceremony. Dona Cinotta may be able to help you. She is a healer of souls. In any case it will do you good to go and see her.

You have several exasperated emails from your boss asking you to contact a client urgently. Things are getting hot for you. You don't have time here to settle the matter, but once you get to Temoaya you'll have to take the time to compose an email diplomatic enough to buy time on that contract. If you care about still having a job.
Otherwise, Riwan has left you a message: say hello to Emilie for him, if you find her.
You go back to your table with a sigh.

This time Lucas invites you to meet him at his flat. He lives in a relatively modern block in one of Mexico City's middle-class suburbs, about twenty minutes by metro. The neighbourhood is quiet; you tell yourself that if a policeman is willing to live here the place must be safe.
As soon as he greets you on the landing, Lucas seems relaxed and does everything to put you at ease. You can also tell he isn't on his first drink, and his first reflex is to pour you one so as to share the bottle open on the coffee table. The flat is rather smart, but Lucas complains about his lot as an ordinary cop, about the ban on using air conditioning, about his noisy, dirty neighbours…
Back then — before the revolution — a policeman could hope for plenty of bonuses depending on his results. He used them to build up a small personal arsenal which he shows you with pride. He extols his HK 416 F, a German assault rifle used in Europe, its lightness, its accuracy. The Mexican police are no longer allowed to carry weapons on ordinary duty. Lucas gets worked up, declaring that the scum has won in Mexico, that the government has quietly restarted drug production and is enriching itself that way, that it has thrown the doors wide open to the feminazis condemned by European justice.
You aren't surprised by this line, but it makes you uncomfortable. Lucas insists that all the volunteers must be thrown out, kicked out, or eliminated if need be. Aware that he may have been tactless, and despite his drunkenness, he adds that fortunately there are patriots like you who come to bring their children back to reason, and that this is also why he wants to help you. He pours you another glass. But he would rather warn you: most of the girls who land in Mexico end up dykes, or go off to Africa pregnant in a Congolese man's luggage. The policeman heaves a sigh and turns towards a photograph taped to the wall. If only he came back, all this would change, he lets slip.
You know the figure on that poster: Guzman Jr, the son of a former drug baron. Exiled to the United States, he obtained his father's parole in exchange, apparently, for a promise to fight for freedom and democracy in Mexico. In Emilie's mind, Guzman Jr was the perfect symbol of the perversion of Western capitalism. And even if you refused to concede the point, you have to admit your daughter didn't talk only nonsense. Those spats with her are, incidentally, one of the things you miss most…
Finally Lucas absolutely insists on showing you his old riot gear, a fairly standard navy-blue outfit. He runs an insistent finger over the death's-head patch embroidered on the shoulder, and the slogan in English: GOD WILL JUDGE OUR ENEMIES – WE WILL ARRANGE THE MEETING.
It is more than time to bring the conversation back to your business… to begin with, you take stock of all the information you have gathered since your excursion to Temoaya. You then ask Lucas whether he has found a lead to Emilie. He drops the jacket and settles on a stool. Yes, of course, he has good news. He's a real cop, efficient. He has learned that Emilie went to the central hospital in Mexico City. But he doesn't know why. He will go on making enquiries. You can always take a trip to the hospital if you feel like it, but the most likely thing is that they'll tell you nothing.

As affable as ever, Juan listens attentively to the account of your search.
He promises to do what he can to help you, by activating his contacts in Mexico City. But he promises nothing. In any case, he doesn't let you go until you have accepted a dinner invitation. He is moving in with his partner, Cassandra, and he insists that you spend an evening with them.

The nurses are not much more forthcoming about the doctor. They confirm that Dr Santorini does indeed practise here, in plastic and reconstructive surgery, but it isn't possible to arrange a meeting for you. They make it clear that if your daughter fled to Mexico it was no doubt for a good reason. They quite understand your sadness, but her decision must be respected too…
A young man in fatigues approaches you, hands clasped behind his back. It seems you are now the centre of general attention in this almost empty hospital lobby. Embarrassed, you put Emilie's photograph back in your pocket and leave.
You will get nothing here.

You spend a pleasant evening. Juan and his partner live in a fairly spacious flat in the La Roma district. They are in the middle of moving in together, as the entrance hall testifies, cluttered with piles of boxes not yet unpacked. The interior is furnished but rather sparse for now.
Cassandra has made tortillas stuffed with cheese and minced meat, with a salad and guacamole. It's rather good, but you find yourself reflecting that you would probably have prepared something along the same lines. That isn't surprising: neither of your two hosts is Mexican by origin. The conversation turns first on fairly simple subjects, then on what you think of your stay in Mexico in particular. You try to avoid remarks that might wound, but you feel clearly that Juan hopes you will praise the achievements of the Mexican Socialist Party. Cassandra seems a little more withdrawn, while her man insistently emphasises the part she played in the volunteers' battles against the drug cartels.
He gets up to rummage in a box and brings out a framed photo showing Cassandra in military dress, posing beside Fîrya Behwan. You know the icon of the Mexican Revolution; Emilie had a poster of her on her wall, and you know the little it is useful to know about her. She fled Rojava after the annihilation of the Kurdish state by the Turks, and reached Mexico; it was she who coordinated the armed force made up of volunteers, and a great share of the credit for their victory is attributed to her. Shortly after the formation of the Socialist Republic, Behwan was assassinated in Mexico City by a far-right group which some claim was backed by the Americans. From then on she did not have to shoulder the Party's policies, and that is doubtless what explains the considerable popularity she enjoys among European youth.
You slightly exaggerate your astonishment at this photograph and Juan answers with a radiant smile. He seems lost in his daydreams, while Cassandra, irritated, taps on the tablecloth. Finally she gets up to clear the table and, as if woken by that movement, he comes back to his place at the table. He fixes you intently in the eyes and pours you a glass of pulque.
"So, comrade, let's come back to your daughter. I imagine that concerns you more than the Revolution…"
If you have gathered two clues, each corresponding to a number, which seem essential to your search, you can tell him about them.

Choice.text: Tell him about the two clues you have gathered
Choice.ask: Add the two numbers together. Which paragraph do you get?

Page.Text:
You take stock with Juan, but neither he nor you has made any progress. Noting your nervousness, the young man lays a friendly hand on your arm.
"Don't worry, and above all don't listen to the birds of ill omen… it isn't all rosy here, but I'm sure your daughter is managing. From what you've told me, she's resourceful. And there's always room in Mexico for girls like her. You have to keep at it! Maybe you need to spend more time understanding our country… understanding her. I believe in it!
And who knows, in the end, maybe you'll come to grow fond of Mexico…"
